printed_headline_estimate: Section 4 (1991 small-house central water share outcome, N = 351 MCAs in 55 urban areas; Tables 4a-5 prose, PDF pp. 8, 23-27): OLS strategic-interaction slope beta = -0.43 on opponent localities' 1980 water servicing W'b (spatial MLE beta = -0.53) and negative ln(income) x ln(urban households) interaction (-0.0261 in Table 4a fn. 13, PDF p. 25; -0.0982 in Table 5 col 3, PDF p. 27; formatted table pages 39-46 blank in PDF text layer). Section 5 (1991-2000 locality urban household growth outcome d ln L, N = 351 MCAs; Table 7 prose, PDF pp. 32-33): 2SLS beta = 0.74 on 1991 small-house water servicing (0.77 with shorter instrument list, p < 0.10, p > 0.05, first-stage F ~ 13; untitled-house water share robustness LIML beta = 1.82, SE = 2.22). Appendix A (1980 hedonic log-rent outcome; Table A1 prose, PDF p. 10): central water rent premium = 12% (Sao Paulo) and 23% (Rio de Janeiro).
publication_year_note: NBER Working Paper No. 14136, printed date June 2008 and copyright 2008 (working paper; no journal volume/issue year appears on the PDF).
rationale: The full 50-page NBER working paper text (June 2008) is readable in prose (though the appended formatted table/figure pages at PDF pp. 39-46, 48, and 50 are blank in the PDF text layer, every specification and variable is fully detailed in Sections 2-5 and Appendix A). Although the paper conducts multiple inferential econometric analyses (OLS, spatial MLE, 2SLS, LIML), none tests a narrow Criterion 2 rule-type legal/tenure/tariff/ownership/regulatory exposure on a Criterion 4 water/sanitation service access outcome: (1) Section 4 (Tables 4a-6) models the 1991 share of small (1-3 room) houses with a central water connection (Criterion 4), but the explanatory variables are neighboring localities' water coverage rates (W'b reaction-function slope), log median household income, log number of urban households, their wealth-by-size interaction, population density, and 1982 anti-military legislative vote share—socioeconomic, demographic, partisan-voting, and spatial-lag predictors rather than a rule-type legal, tenure, zoning, tariff, or ownership variable (pre-1988 national illegality of servicing informal settlements is nationwide background context and not a regression variable); (2) Section 5 (Tables 7-8) reverses the exposure-outcome relationship by using 1991 water servicing of small (or untitled) houses as the predictor of 1991-2000 locality urban household growth (failing Criterion 4); (3) Appendix A (Table A1) estimates hedonic log-rent regressions measuring consumer willingness-to-pay for water/sewer connections (explicitly failing Criterion 4); (4) Appendix B (Table B2) first-stage regressions predict water servicing from porous geology, solar insolation, distance to Sao Paulo, and 1970 census demographics (failing Criterion 2); and (5) Tables 1-3 are purely descriptive cross-tabulations (Table 3 examines municipal minimum lot-size laws >125 m2 only against descriptive migrant and untitled-homeowner ratios, with no water/sanitation outcome).
